seo.title: Internal Linking for AI Search: A Practical Guide
seo.meta_description: Internal linking for AI search: how links help crawlers and AI tools find and understand your pages, anchor text, hub structure and common mistakes to fix.

h1: Internal Linking for AI Search: Help Crawlers and AI Understand Your Site
answer: Internal linking for AI search means connecting your pages with clear, crawlable links so search engines and AI crawlers can discover every important page and understand how topics relate. Google says it generally can only crawl links that are HTML anchor elements with an href. Use descriptive anchor text, link hubs to detailed pages and back, and keep key pages a few clicks from the homepage.
key_takeaways: Crawlers discover pages by following links.
Google generally only crawls a links with an href attribute.
Descriptive anchor text explains what the linked page is about.
Hubs and clusters show how topics fit together.
Orphan pages may never be found or cited.

sections.heading: Why internal links matter for AI
sections.body_html: AI tools that search the web depend on crawlers and indexes. A page that no other page links to, often called an orphan page, may be discovered late or not at all, even if it is listed in a sitemap. Internal links also carry meaning: they tell crawlers which pages are important and how pages relate. For AI answers built from several related searches, a well-linked cluster of pages makes it easier for each relevant page to be found.

sections.heading: Make links crawlable
sections.body_html: Google's link best practices say it can generally only crawl a link if it is an <a> HTML element with an href attribute, and that most links in other formats will not be parsed. Navigation built only with JavaScript click handlers, buttons that change pages without real links, or links that only appear after user interaction may be missed. Check that your important links are plain anchor elements in the HTML.

sections.heading: Write descriptive anchor text
sections.body_html: Anchor text is the clickable text of a link. Google recommends that it be descriptive and make sense out of context. "Click here" and "read more" tell nobody anything. "How much GEO costs" or "our robots.txt guide for AI crawlers" tells both readers and crawlers what to expect. Use natural phrases, vary them, and avoid stuffing keywords into every anchor.

sections.heading: Structure: hubs, clusters and the homepage
sections.body_html:
• Homepage links to your main service pages and topic hubs.
  • Hub pages introduce a topic and link to every detailed page in it.
  • Detailed pages link back to their hub and to closely related pages.
  • Service pages link to the guides that answer pre-purchase questions, and guides link to the relevant service.

This structure keeps important pages close to the homepage and makes relationships obvious.

sections.heading: Contextual links inside content
sections.body_html: Links placed within the body of a page, where they naturally help the reader, carry clear context. When a guide mentions a concept that another page explains in depth, link to it there. Aim for links that a reader would genuinely want to follow; a handful of relevant contextual links per page is usually more useful than long lists.

sections.heading: Find and fix orphan pages
sections.body_html:
1. Export the URLs in your sitemap.
  2. Crawl your site with a crawler tool to see which pages are linked internally.
  3. Compare the lists: sitemap pages that the crawl did not find are orphans.
  4. Link each orphan from its hub and from one or two related pages, or remove it if it has no purpose.

sections.heading: Pages outside the main menu
sections.body_html: Not every page needs to be in the navigation menu. Guides can live outside the menu as long as they are reachable through links from hubs, related pages, an index page or the homepage. A clear hub page that lists all guides, linked from the homepage, is a simple way to keep many pages discoverable without crowding the menu.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body_html:
• Linking only through JavaScript or images without proper anchor elements.
  • Generic anchors such as "here" everywhere.
  • Broken links after URLs change, without redirects.
  • Important pages buried many clicks deep.
  • Huge footer link blocks instead of contextual links.

sections.heading: Maintenance
sections.body_html: Each time you publish a new page, add links to it from its hub and from two or three related existing pages, and link from it to relevant pages. Run a broken-link check monthly, and update links when you merge or move content. Internal linking is never finished; it grows with the site.

sections.heading: How to check the effect
sections.body_html: In Search Console, new pages that are well linked tend to be discovered and indexed sooner. Track how quickly new pages show impressions, whether orphan pages begin to appear after you link them, and whether AI tools cite more of your cluster pages for related questions.

sections.heading: An example link plan for one cluster
sections.body_html: Imagine a cluster on AI crawler access. The hub page explains AI crawlers in general and links to four detailed pages: a list of crawler user agents, a robots.txt guide, an llms.txt guide and a firewall troubleshooting guide. Each detailed page links back to the hub near the top or in its introduction, links to the other cluster pages where they are mentioned, and links to the related service page in its conclusion. The homepage links to the hub. Every page is reachable within two clicks of the homepage, and every link explains where it leads.

sections.heading: Links between services and guides
sections.body_html: Guides attract people who are researching; service pages convert people who are ready. Link from each guide to the service that solves its problem, and from each service page to the two or three guides that answer common pre-purchase questions. This helps buyers move naturally from learning to contacting you, and helps crawlers understand which guides support which services.

faqs.q: Why does internal linking matter for AI search?
faqs.a: Crawlers discover and understand pages through links. Well-linked pages are found sooner and their relationships are clearer, which helps AI tools that rely on search indexes.
Google says it can generally only crawl links that are HTML anchor elements with an href attribute. Links in other formats are usually not parsed.
Descriptive text that tells readers and crawlers what the linked page is about, such as "how much GEO costs" instead of "click here".
A page with no internal links pointing to it. It may be discovered late or not at all, even if it is in the sitemap.

faqs.q: Do pages need to be in the main menu to be found?
faqs.a: No. Pages can be reached through links from hubs, related pages or an index page linked from the homepage.

faqs.q: How many internal links should a page have?
faqs.a: There is no fixed number. Include links that genuinely help readers move to related topics; a few relevant contextual links are usually enough.

faqs.q: How often should I review internal links?
faqs.a: Add links whenever you publish, and run a broken-link check about once a month.

faqs.q: Do internal links help pages get cited by AI?
faqs.a: Indirectly. Links help crawlers find and understand pages, which is a precondition for being indexed and therefore available to AI tools that rely on search indexes.
